statement: Design a stack that supports **push**, **pop**, **top**, **peekMax** (the largest element) and **popMax** (remove and return the largest element; if several are equal, the one nearest the top).

flaw.ctx: You asked for a max stack with an efficient popMax.
flaw.answer: Correct results, false complexity claim. `Max()` and `LastIndexOf` scan the whole list and `RemoveAt` shifts it: PeekMax and PopMax are **O(n)**, so n PopMax calls are O(n²). Worth knowing: .NET vectorises `Max` and `LastIndexOf` with SIMD, so at 100,000 elements this finishes in under 3 seconds and looks fine — it takes 300,000 to expose it. A benchmark at one size is not a complexity proof.
flaw.fix: A doubly linked list for order plus a `SortedSet<(value, seq)>` — PopMax O(log n).
flaw.verified: compiled against this problem's stage tests by npm run verify

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Design a stack that supports **push**, **pop**, **top**, **peekMax** (the largest element) and **popMax** (remove and return the largest element; if several are equal, the one nearest the top).

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- What do pop/top/peekMax/popMax do on an empty stack? (The tests expect `InvalidOperationException`.)
- With duplicate maxima, which one does popMax remove? (The topmost.)
- What complexity is expected for popMax? (Say O(n) for two stacks before you improve it.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Two stacks give O(1) peekMax but O(n) popMax, because the max can be buried. A linked list gives O(1) removal of a node you hold; a sorted set keyed by (value, insertion sequence) gives you that node for the topmost maximum in O(log n).

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: I would say, before coding: "A." doubly linked list for stack order plus a SortedSet of (value, sequence) makes PopMax O(log n), where the two-stack approach makes it O(n)."

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md: Two stacks give O(1) peekMax but O(n) popMax, because the max can be buried. A linked list gives O(1) removal of a node you hold; a sorted set keyed by (value, insertion sequence) gives you that node for the topmost maximum in O(log n).

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Make the design decision yourself, then ask the assistant to attack it.
- Delegate the mechanical parts only after the structure is fixed.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe a doubly linked list for stack order plus a SortedSet of (value, sequence) makes PopMax O(log n), where the two-stack approach makes it O(n). Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call Push, Pop and PopMax concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."
- *Requirement change* — "The requirement changed: PopMax must be better than O(n). The test pushes 300,000 values and pops the max 300,000 times within a time limit. List which members need to change and which do not, before writing any code."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- The two-stack solution presented as O(1) popMax.
- Removing the bottom-most duplicate maximum instead of the topmost.
- An int sequence counter on a long-lived stack (use long).
- Unlinking the node but forgetting to remove it from the sorted set (or vice versa).

**Verification exercise:** Incorrect complexity — Correct results, false complexity claim. `Max()` and `LastIndexOf` scan the whole list and `RemoveAt` shifts it: PeekMax and PopMax are **O(n)**, so n PopMax calls are O(n²). Worth knowing: .NET vectorises `Max` and `LastIndexOf` with SIMD, so at 100,000 elements this finishes in under 3 seconds and looks fine — it takes 300,000 to expose it. A benchmark at one size is not a complexity proof.
